To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

loss of heterozygois (LOH), TP53 mutations, and P53 protein overexpression were detected in lip squamous cell carcinomas (LSCC), and that TP53 mutations were also detected in actinic cheilitiis (AC), a premalignant condition.
loss of heterozygozity and TP53 mutations are common in lip cancer and actinic cheilities, but BRAF V600 mutations are rare in these lesions.
LOH and TP553 mutations are common in LSCC but BRAF V600 mutations are rare.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic mechanisms of LSCC and actinic cheiliitis.
the molecular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of LSCC and actinic cheilosis.
the genetic alterations of the TP53 gene in LSCC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LOH at 9p and 17p and TP53 mutations are involved in lip carcinogenesis.
LSCC and actinic cheilosis are genetically different, but share common features.
the genetic alterations found in LSCC are similar to those found in AC, and are similar to those described in other head and neck SCC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LOH and TP 53 mutations may be associated with LSCC pathogenic mechanisms, whereas BRAF mutations are not.
TP53 mutation and LOH at 9p and 9q, but not at 17p, are common events in LSCC.
TP53 and BRAV600E mutations are not associated to lip cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LSCC and its precursor lesions are characterized by frequent LOH and TP3 mutations.

the genetic mechanisms involved in the development of lip cancer are not different from those involved in other head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, but the low incidence of the disease makes the study of this cancer difficult.
the molecular mechanisms of LSCC and actinic cheilosis are similar, and that the TP53 gene is the main target of UV-induced DNA damage in the lip.
